clue.text: It has circle, it has rings!

indicators.note: the first piece holds on to the second, so they sit side by side

parts.note: 'it' is old slang for sex appeal, abbreviated SA
to circle is to go round, to turn

explanation.surface: An excited cry about something round and ringed, like a hoop or a target.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'it's read as pronouns; the first is the old slang for sex appeal ('she's got it'), while the second half, 'it has rings', is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: this planet is the one best known for its bright ring system.

clue.text: Drink and flirt?

definitions.meaning: a flirt as a person: a slick, silver-tongued charmer

explanation.surface: Someone at a bar wonders whether to order a drink and chat somebody up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flirt' is a noun here, a person who flirts, which is what lets it match a smoothie in the smooth-talker sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A smoothie is both a blended fruit drink and an informal word for a slick, charming man.

clue.text: Blunted needles applied to joint, immediate and painful punishment

indicators.note: the needles are put next to the joint, so the pieces sit side by side

parts.note: something blunted has been cut short
sharps = needles, as in a hospital sharps bin
the hock is the ankle joint of a horse's hind leg

explanation.surface: A grim scene of blunt needles being stuck into a joint as some cruel, swift penalty.
explanation.walkthrough: The split runs across the words of the answer: SHARPS gives the S that starts SHOCK. 'Short, sharp shock' is a British phrase for a brief, harsh punishment, famously for young offenders.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: a short, sharp shock is a quick, severe punishment meant to deter.

clue.text: Book opened by English and Greek character, classic example

parts.note: E = English
pi is a letter of the Greek alphabet
a tome is a large book

explanation.surface: A classic book whose first page begins with English and Greek writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' comes first in the clue but last in the answer: being 'opened by' the other pieces puts it at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word names the one instance that sums up a whole type perfectly.

clue.text: Not the winner, though hardly puffing?

definitions.meaning: reads as a plain runner-up; really one who nearly won
reads as not out of breath; really not smoking the prize

explanation.surface: A runner-up who finished without even being out of breath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puffing' pretends to mean panting from effort, but it is puffing on a cigar, the old fairground prize a near-miss didn't win.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom said of an attempt that nearly succeeds but just falls short of the prize.

clue.text: Ultimately impressive, say, property bequeathed

indicators.note: in the end, so take the final letter

parts.note: last letter of impressivE
to state = to say

explanation.surface: Someone remarks on an impressive inheritance of property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' reads as 'for example' in the surface; it is really the verb to state.
explanation.definitionFit: An estate is all the property a person leaves to be passed on at death.

clue.text: Unidentified humanoid in spirit eyed up

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the next words
in a down clue, reading upward turns the letters round

parts.note: spirIT EYed

explanation.surface: An unknown creature is glimpsed by someone who has been drinking spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' is a natural hint at a ghost, but it only carries letters here.
explanation.definitionFit: The yeti is the unconfirmed ape-like creature said to roam the Himalayas.

clue.text: Symbol of victory in hand?

definitions.note: 'in hand' points to a part of the hand rather than the whole
definitions.meaning: winners in ancient games were handed a frond from this tree
the flat inner surface of the hand

explanation.surface: A winner holding a trophy in their hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the loose second half: the palm is a part of the hand rather than a synonym for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Palm fronds were given to victors in ancient times, and the palm is the flat inside of the hand.

clue.text: Swinging joint

definitions.meaning: swinging = fashionable, as in the swinging sixties
a joint of the body, at the top of the leg

explanation.surface: A joint that swings, like a hinge or a limb.
explanation.walkthrough: Read together, 'swinging joint' sounds like a hinge or a lively nightclub; split, it is two separate meanings of HIP.
explanation.definitionFit: Hip means trendy, like 'swinging', and it is also the ball-and-socket joint at the top of the leg.

clue.text: Look here where inlets forming

indicators.note: the letters are being formed into something new

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A guide points to a spot on the coast where small bays are taking shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look here' is not about seeing: it is the interjection that demands attention, just as 'Listen!' does.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Look here!' and 'Listen!' are both said to make someone pay attention.

clue.text: Jokes I'm not sure written in time

parts.note: an hour is a unit of time
um is the noise of hesitation

explanation.surface: A comedian pencils in some jokes at the last minute, doubtful they will land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm not sure' is a whole phrase standing for the hesitant sound UM.
explanation.definitionFit: Humour means jokes and comic material in general.

clue.text: Island state, like isle I observed in word of gratitude

indicators.note: the pieces are seen inside the word of thanks

parts.note: ta = thanks, informal British
as = like
the Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea
I as itself

explanation.surface: A traveller says thank you on arriving at an island state that resembles another island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Island state' reads as a nation like Malta; here it is a state within a federal country. Everything between 'Island state,' and 'in' goes inside the thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: this island off the south of Australia is one of that country's six states.

clue.text: Air's beneath them circulating, at once

indicators.note: moving round, so the letters are stirred

parts.note: anagram fodder, 15 letters

explanation.surface: Air moves beneath birds' or planes' wings as they fly.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'Air's' is ignored; its S is part of the fodder. Air and breath make the surface quietly fit the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: to say two things in the same breath is to say them at once.

clue.text: Greek letter, that afore upsilon, originally

definitions.text: Greek letter, that afore upsilon, originally

indicators.note: originally means at the origin, so each word gives its first letter

parts.note: the opening letters of that, afore and upsilon

explanation.surface: A note on the Greek alphabet: this letter comes just before upsilon.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: tau really is the letter immediately before upsilon in the Greek alphabet. Afore is an old word for before.
explanation.definitionFit: Tau is the nineteenth letter of the Greek alphabet, sitting right before upsilon.

clue.text: Cat — or weasel, by the sound of it?

indicators.note: judge by how it is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: a weasel is a sly, cheating person; CHEATER said in a non-rhotic accent

explanation.surface: Someone can't tell whether an animal is a cat or a weasel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weasel' wants to be another animal next to 'cat'; it is really a sly, untrustworthy person, a cheater.
explanation.definitionFit: The cheetah is the big cat famed as the fastest land animal.

clue.text: Success impacted

definitions.meaning: a smash success, as with a chart-topping song
impacted = struck, the past tense of a verb of striking

explanation.surface: A success that made a real impact.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words are different parts of speech: 'Success' is a noun, 'impacted' a past-tense verb, and one short word covers both.
explanation.definitionFit: A hit is a success, and hit also means struck or impacted.

clue.text: Being discussed, a number of lies?

parts.note: A as itself
from the set phrase for a web of falsehoods, 'a ___ of lies'

explanation.surface: A debate in which several untruths come up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A tissue of lies' is a set phrase for a web of falsehoods, so a tissue is a collection of lies.
explanation.definitionFit: A matter at issue is the one under discussion or in dispute.

clue.text: He philosophised like that over cases

parts.note: so = in that way
crates are packing cases

explanation.surface: A thinker argues his point in exactly that way over several cases.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cases' sounds like legal or philosophical arguments; they are packing boxes.
explanation.definitionFit: Socrates was the Athenian philosopher famous for questioning people.

clue.text: Damaging plug, number of lines

parts.note: a plug is a bit of advertising, an ad
a verse is a group of lines in a poem

explanation.surface: A harmful advertisement written as a few lines of poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plug' reads as a stopper; it is the verb-turned-noun for promoting something.
explanation.definitionFit: Adverse means harmful or damaging, as in adverse effects.

clue.text: Poor introduction from Stevenson, Kidnapped?

indicators.note: the opening letter of the word

parts.note: first letter of Stevenson
a kidnap victim is trapped for cash, held to ransom

explanation.surface: A reader finds the opening of Robert Louis Stevenson's novel Kidnapped disappointing.
explanation.walkthrough: Kidnapped is Stevenson's novel, but here it is the plain verb: someone kidnapped is held, trapped, for a ransom in cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Being strapped for cash means being short of money, poor.

clue.text: Wales is windy, and centre of England too

indicators.note: a windy route twists about, so the letters of Wales are blown around and rearranged
the centre of the seven-letter word England is its fourth letter

parts.note: L is the middle letter of England

explanation.surface: A weather complaint: Wales is blustery, and the middle of England is as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'windy' looks like weather, but it is the signal to rearrange WALES; 'centre of England' supplies the final L.
explanation.definitionFit: As well and too are interchangeable adverbs meaning in addition or also.

clue.text: Proust lost in brain fog

indicators.note: the letters have lost their way

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Marcel Proust, the novelist of memory, drifting in a mental haze.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface nods to Proust's In Search of Lost Time, a novel all about memory.
explanation.definitionFit: A stupor is a dazed state where the mind is fogged.

clue.text: When so, so devious, is it something akin to a racket?

indicators.note: going by a winding route, so the letters wander

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a shady scheme counts as a racket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Racket' pretends to be a scam; it is the tennis kind. A snowshoe is a racket-shaped frame strung with webbing, worn to walk on snow.
explanation.definitionFit: Traditional snowshoes are frames with laced webbing, much like a tennis racket.

clue.text: Bread that also may rise?

parts.note: a leavened bread rises in the oven, and in a down entry this word, read upwards, is the same word again

explanation.surface: A baker's question about a loaf that might puff up as well.
explanation.walkthrough: Bread dough rises, but 'may rise' is also about the grid: in a down entry, reading the four letters upwards gives the same word, as with a palindrome.
explanation.definitionFit: Naan is a leavened flatbread from South Asian cooking, baked in a tandoor oven.

clue.text: Reckless winger invariably costing Arsenal, result uplifting Spurs, initially

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each of the six words gives its first letter

parts.words: invariably costing Arsenal, result uplifting Spurs
parts.note: the first letters of invariably, costing, Arsenal, result, uplifting and Spurs

explanation.surface: A football report: a reckless winger keeps costing Arsenal, to the delight of rivals Tottenham Hotspur, known as Spurs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'winger' suggests a footballer, but here it is a mythical flier on wax wings.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Icarus flew too near the sun on wings of wax and fell, a byword for recklessness.

clue.text: Bulb I left in bank, screwed back

indicators.note: twisted round backwards, so the whole thing is reversed

parts.note: a crag is a steep rocky bank
I as itself
L = left

explanation.surface: Someone planting a bulb in a riverbank and twisting it back into the earth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bulb' sounds like a light bulb screwed into a socket, but it is a plant bulb, the kind split into cloves.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a head of this plant is a bulb made up of cloves.

clue.text: Country dropping off in spring

indicators.note: a word dropping off another falls away from it, so those letters are removed from the country

parts.note: Spain is the country of the Iberian peninsula
the word in itself, taken out of the country's name

explanation.surface: A country nodding off during springtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping off' suggests falling asleep, but it removes IN from SPAIN; 'spring' is not the season but a source of water.
explanation.definitionFit: A spa is a mineral spring whose waters are thought to be healthy, as at the Belgian town of that name.

clue.text: Some lover, ostensibly?

indicators.note: only some of the letters are used

parts.note: lovER OStensibly

explanation.surface: Someone who appears to be in love, at least on the face of it.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue also defines: the god of love is 'some lover' on the face of it, and the question mark admits the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Eros is the Greek god of erotic love, a lover par excellence.
